passage: On the terrace of the Andheri flat, someone had put on music, and Karan had a plate of samosas and a joke. "Women drivers," he said, spinning an imaginary steering wheel. "Left indicator, turns right." Two of the boys laughed. Pooja, holding a paper cup, gave the small tight smile Naveen had seen her use at the office when she didn't want a scene. Naveen felt the laugh sitting in his own throat. He put down his plate. "Karan, Pooja drove all four of us back from Lonavala in the rain last month, and I fell asleep in the front seat. Sounds like decent driving to me." His voice was steady. "That joke's old." Karan blinked, then shrugged. "Okay, okay." The music changed. Pooja looked at Naveen and mouthed, "Thanks."

qa.q: Who drove the four of them back from Lonavala?
qa.a: Pooja drove all four of them back from Lonavala in the rain.

qa.q: What is Naveen feeling as the laugh sits in his throat?
qa.a: Naveen feels uncomfortable and torn. He does not want to laugh along, yet he is also nervous about speaking.

qa.q: What choice did Naveen make, and why might it have worked?
qa.a: He put down his plate and spoke calmly, using a real memory of Pooja's driving, so it sounded like a fact and not a lecture.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when Naveen speaks?
qa.a: Grateful and relieved. She had been putting up with the joke behind a tight smile, and she mouths "Thanks" afterwards.

grounding: A young man hears a friend joke about women drivers and chooses to object calmly in the moment rather than laugh.

passage: "Did you see the news about that case?" Dev said, grinning. "Honestly, some rape jokes write themselves." A couple of people snickered. Swati looked down at her laptop. Rehan put his cup down. "Dev, I'm not laughing at that one." "Relax, it's just a joke." "Maybe. But it's about something that happens to real people. I'd rather not hear it." The room went quiet. Dev raised his hands. "Fine, fine. You've gone serious on us." "Maybe I have," Rehan said, and turned back to his screen. His heart was thumping. Ten minutes later Swati stopped by his desk. "Thanks for that." "I nearly kept quiet," he admitted. "I know. Nobody does it easily."

passage:
We were at Samir's birthday, six of us boys around a table of kebabs, when Samir told a joke about a woman who couldn't park. Everyone laughed. Then he told another one, a rape joke, the kind I'd heard a hundred times and laughed at to fit in.
This time I didn't laugh. I thought of my sister, who takes two buses home after dark.
The table went quiet around me. Samir said, "Arre, Kishore, it's a joke, yaar."
I kept my voice easy. "I know, bhai. It's just not funny to me. Tell the one about your driving test instead."
For a second nobody moved. Then someone laughed, at Samir's driving test, and the talk moved on.
Later, one of the others texted me: "Glad you said that. I didn't know how." Looking back, that text mattered more than the silence.

qa.q: Whose birthday was it?
qa.a: It was Samir's birthday.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he didn't laugh?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and protective, thinking of his sister who takes two buses home after dark.

qa.q: What made Kishore's response work?
qa.a: He stayed calm and friendly, said the joke wasn't funny to him without lecturing, and offered a new topic so the group could move on.

qa.q: How might Samir feel when the table goes quiet?
qa.a: Samir may feel embarrassed and defensive, which is why he says it's just a joke, but he also learns the group won't simply laugh along.

grounding: A young man hears friends' jokes about women drivers and rape, chooses to calmly object in the moment, and shifts what the group accepts.

passage:
Team lead's note, Thursday.
At lunch in the canteen today, one of the junior engineers made a joke about women and rape. Several people laughed. Shalini, who sits on that table, looked down at her plate.
Chinmay, 24, who joined in March, put his spoon down and said, calmly, "Not okay, man. Let's not." He didn't raise his voice. The one who told the joke said, "Relax, it's just a joke." Chinmay replied, "Still not okay." Then he asked Shalini about her project demo, as if nothing had happened.
I watched the table after that. Nobody told another joke of that kind.
Next step: I spoke privately with the engineer who told the joke, explained why it was harmful, and reminded him of our conduct policy. I also thanked Chinmay, and asked Shalini if she wanted to talk; she said she was fine but appreciated it.

qa.q: What did Chinmay say when told to relax?
qa.a: Chinmay replied, "Still not okay."

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling when he put his spoon down?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable and determined, noticing Shalini look down, but calm enough to object without raising his voice.

qa.q: Why was it helpful for Chinmay to then ask Shalini about her demo?
qa.a: It moved the conversation on and treated Shalini as a colleague rather than a topic, without turning the moment into a big scene.

qa.q: How might Shalini have experienced the lunch?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and uncomfortable when the joke was told, and was likely relieved that someone objected so she didn't have to.

grounding: A note-writer records a young man calmly objecting to a rape joke at lunch, and how that shifts what the group accepts.

passage:
Friday
Office outing to the bowling alley. Rakesh and the boys from sales started on "women drivers" when Noor mentioned she'd driven in from Thane. Big laughs. She laughed too, but she stopped talking after that.
I laughed at the first one. I hate that I did.
At the second one I said, "Come on, she drove forty kilometres in traffic and got here before us. Maybe we're the bad drivers." A couple of people actually laughed at that instead. Rakesh rolled his eyes.
On the way out, Noor said quietly, "Thanks, Santosh bhai." That's all. But she was back to talking in the cab.
Note to self: next time, the first joke. Not the second. It's easier than I thought. My hands were shaking and nobody even noticed.
— Santosh

qa.q: Where had Noor driven in from?
qa.a: Noor had driven in from Thane.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after laughing at the first joke?
qa.a: Santosh felt ashamed, writing that he hates that he laughed, and nervous when he did speak up, with his hands shaking.

qa.q: What could Santosh do differently next time?
qa.a: He could object at the first joke rather than the second, calmly and with humour, as he did when he pointed out Noor's drive.

qa.q: How was Noor affected by the jokes and by Santosh speaking up?
qa.a: She stopped talking after the jokes, which suggests she felt belittled, but after Santosh spoke she thanked him and was back to talking in the cab.

grounding: A young man hears colleagues joke about women drivers, regrets laughing, and then calmly objects, shifting the group's mood.

passage:
Boys' group chat, Friday night.
Divyansh: saw a lady take 5 mins to park outside the mall 😅 this is why women shouldn't get licences
Rohit: haha
Divyansh: Akash where's your laugh
Akash: Nah. My sister drives me to work every day and hasn't scraped once. I've scraped twice.
Divyansh: bro it's a joke
Akash: I know. Just not a funny one to me. The lady was probably just parking carefully.
(Three minutes of nothing.)
Sameer: honestly my mum is the best driver in our house
Rohit: ok fair, my brother failed his test twice
Divyansh: fine fine. Akash, you're driving to the match tomorrow then 🙂
Akash: Deal. Pick you up at 4.

qa.q: Who drives Akash to work every day?
qa.a: His sister drives him to work every day.

qa.q: Why did Akash refuse to laugh, and what might he have felt typing his reply?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable with a joke that mocked women and probably a little nervous about spoiling the mood, yet sure enough to say so calmly.

qa.q: What made Akash's reply work in the group?
qa.a: He stayed calm, used a real example and did not insult Divyansh, so Sameer and Rohit felt free to agree instead of taking sides.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt when nobody replied for three minutes?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt awkward and a bit exposed, then eased the tension by joking that Akash should drive, a sign he had taken the point.

grounding: It illustrates a young man who hears a joke about women drivers in a group chat and calmly objects, shifting what the group will laugh at.
